title: A retry need not create another record
audience: A new engineer learning to read request traces
question: Why do two requests leave only one stored record in this example?
summary: The fictional register reuses a receipt for a repeated key: 2 requests, 1 stored record.
context: Explicitly fictional, sequential teaching trace. No implementation was executed.

sources.title: Fictional sequential retry trace
sources.note: Authored input evidence; not production logs. Read events, counts, rule and qualification.

claims.text: Both requests use key K7 and receive receipt R9.
The trace contains 2 requests and 1 stored record.
claims.scope: Counts in this trace, not a throughput measurement.

claims.text: A repeated key can reuse a result without another write in this register.
claims.basis: The supplied rule and second receipt agree with the single stored record.
claims.uncertainty: This sequential example does not establish crash safety or behavior under concurrent requests.

beats.title: The same key returns the same receipt
beats.text: Follow K7 through the original request and its retry.
beats.narration: In this fictional trace, a client submits key K7. The register stores one record and returns receipt R9. The client then retries the same key. The register returns the same receipt without another write.

visual.title: One sequential retry
visual.description: The second request repeats K7 and returns R9; the trace contains one store operation.
visual.caption: Source: retry-log, events and rule. Fictional and sequential.

beats.title: Count writes, not just requests
beats.text: Two requests. One stored record. Keep the scope narrow.
beats.narration: Count the requests and records separately: two requests, one stored record. Does that prove crash safety or behavior under concurrent requests? No. This example covers sequential requests only. Its lesson is narrower: a repeated key can reuse a result.

visual.title: Different counts
visual.description: Counted objects differ: requests versus stored records in the same fictional trace.
visual.caption: Source: retry-log, counts. This is not a performance comparison.

question.prompt: Does one stored record prove crash safety or behavior under concurrent requests?
question.answer: No. The supplied trace covers sequential requests only.

limitations: Fictional trace only; concurrency, crashes and persistence are outside its scope.
